transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-11 15:00 PT / Duration ~55m
Attendees: Olivia Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Desai (NovaHealth Head of ML), Evan Ross (NovaHealth Infra), Marta Gomez (NovaHealth Security), Lucas Wei (Product)

00:00 Olivia: hey everyone thanks for joining, we're going to walk through Redwood Optimize focusing on batching and the prefix / KV cache cost model, hope that time still works?
00:07 Priya: yep this is perfect, thanks Olivia, quick context we have two use cases — triage chat for clinicians (short turns, low latency) and a patient intake flow (longer context, many repeated prefixes)
00:18 Marcus: got it, that's a classic mixed workload — we'll talk about per-route SLOs and how batching+cache behave across those distributions
00:26 Evan: just to flag infra constraint, our prod p95 needs to be < 150ms for clinician flow, and we have strict egress rules to your VPC peering
00:36 Marta: also SOC2/AZURE gov questions — can you send KMS/HSM diagrams for private deployment?
00:43 Olivia: yup will share docs after. okay Marcus, take it away
01:00 Marcus: cool — slide 1: batching overview — continuous batching at runtime coalesces requests into micro-batches, we optimize for 1) latency SLOs 2) throughput cost. For short-turn low-latency flows we recommend small concurrency and per-request fast path; for patient intake we can push batch sizes up and enable prefix caching to amortize token compute
01:25 Priya: when you say prefix caching that's the KV cache you mentioned earlier? how persistent is that?
01:32 Marcus: yes prefix or KV cache — it's a lightweight LRU-backed cache of KV pairs for attention keys, TTL configurable. typical pattern: cache user system prompts and common patient history so when the model continues generation it reuses cached KV instead of recomputing prior layers
01:48 Priya: is that safe for PHI? Marta, any thoughts?
01:51 Marta: encryption at rest + customer KMS is required — we'll need key ownership and audit logs, also retention policy — can the cache be flushed on demand?
02:00 Marcus: yes, cache flush and per-tenant namespaces; when using Private or Dedicated you can bring your own KMS and we log cache operations in audit stream
02:12 Lucas: what's the tradeoff, like how much latency saving vs cost increase for cache?
02:18 Marcus: good q. rough rule of thumb: if your average prefix length > 64 tokens and reuse rate > 20%, KV cache can reduce per-request token compute by 30-60% for continuation steps. However there is memory overhead per shard and slight increase in fixed cost if you provision higher cache-backed nodes. That's where the cost model helps
02:38 Olivia: to the cost model — we sent a simplified spreadsheet in advance (link in chat), Marcus can walk through assumptions: base per-token GPU cost, amortized fixed node cost, and cache memory footprint.
02:50 Marcus: slide: cost model assumptions: model variant (base vs quantized int8), tokens per prompt, tokens per completion, average batch coalescing factor, cache hit rate. Example: for clinician flow (avg seq 48 tokens, completions 20 tokens) with small batching (coalescing 1.3x) cost is dominated by latency-optimized smaller batches; patient intake (avg seq 420 tokens) you get big wins with KV cache + batching
03:15 Priya: what's coalescing 1.3x?
03:18 Marcus: it's our observed multiplier — i.e. due to concurrent requests we often group 1.3 requests on average into a compute batch, but that's workload-dependent. For high concurrency webhooks you might see 3-4x
03:28 Evan: do you have a demo or benchmark numbers?
03:32 Marcus: yes here's a benchmark we ran on a 8xA100 pool — clinician flow p50 was 90ms p95 140ms with 1.2x coalescing, patient intake without KV cache p95 was 950ms, with KV cache and batching we drove p95 to 420ms and token cost down ~45%
03:54 Priya: 420ms still feels high for patient intake, but acceptable for async flows; important is predictability and cost.
04:03 Marcus: right — key is to route clinician flow to latency tier (dedicated low-batch nodes) and patient intake to cost tier (higher batch sizes + cache). Redwood routing policies let you do that per-route
04:16 Lucas: what's required to enable KV cache in Private vs Hosted?
04:19 Marcus: hosted supports KV cache as a managed feature with tenant isolation; Private gives you control over cache instance sizing, KMS, and network. For PHI we usually recommend Private or Dedicated with VPC peering and BYOK KMS
04:30 Marta: okay send diagrams. also curious about cache warm-up — cold cache penalties?
04:36 Marcus: cold start happens — for brand new tenants we see the first few requests miss and then warm; you can pre-warm by seeding cache from recent transcripts using our ingest API; warm-up is typically a small fraction of total tokens if you pre-seed
04:49 Priya: can we evict by user or by conversation? some patients have lots of history
04:52 Marcus: eviction policies supported: LRU, TTL, explicit namespaced eviction. you can choose per-route TTLs — longer TTLs increase hit rate but increase memory footprint
05:05 Olivia: let's jump to quantization — often customers trade off some accuracy for cost gains with int8 quantized variants
05:11 Priya: how much quality regression have you observed?
05:14 Marcus: depends on model; for retrieval-augmented or instruction-following small regressions observed on generative nuance tasks; we recommend running evals tied to your prompt sets — Redwood Optimize will surface regression alerts vs baseline when switching quantized models
05:28 Priya: nice — that helps. what's the recommended approach to pick batch sizes?
05:31 Marcus: pick per-route SLO first. for 150ms p95 target, choose small batch ceiling (e.g., 1–4 tokens per batch) with auto-scaling configured. For cost-sensitive routes set batch ceiling higher (8–32) and accept higher latency tails but lower per-token cost. Redwood Console lets you simulate cost vs latency curves for a sample trace
05:50 Evan: can we plug in our real traces?
05:53 Marcus: yes — send us a small sample Prometheus trace or even just a CSV of request timestamps and seq lengths, our cost model notebook will simulate coalescing and cache hit patterns and return estimated per-token $$ and p95 latencies
06:08 Priya: do you model KV cache consistency? e.g., if a clinician updates a chart, how quickly does the cache reflect that?
06:14 Marcus: KV cache is eventually consistent; write-through option available for synchronous updates but that raises latency; typical pattern is event-driven invalidation when chart updates occur — Redwood supports hooks to invalidate keys on your events
06:28 Marta: security question: are cache blobs encrypted per-tenant? where are keys stored?
06:33 Marcus: encrypted at rest; key wrapping via customer KMS for Private / Dedicated; hosted uses our managed KMS but can integrate with BYOK for enterprise contracts
06:44 Lucas: in POC can we test both quantized and full models?
06:47 Olivia: yes, we usually recommend A/B comparing int8 vs fp16 on a small eval set and production-like traces — we'll help automate that with Redwood Optimize
06:56 Priya: any gotchas on batching affecting safety layers or tool calling? we have downstream tool calls that need prompt context
07:03 Marcus: good point — batching should preserve causal ordering and tool-call boundaries; Redwood's runtime ensures per-request token alignment and you can pin routes that use tool calls to non-batched execution if you want strict ordering
07:18 Evan: what's the memory requirement per cached token? rough numbers please
07:22 Marcus: ballpark: for transformer KV pairs about 64 bytes per token per attention head x heads — practical number we use is ~200-350 bytes per cached token depending on model size and kernel packing. So 1M cached tokens -> ~200–350MB; but sharding and compression can reduce that
07:41 Priya: ok so for patient intake at 420 tokens per user and 100k active users that's huge — we need eviction and TTL strategies plus maybe summarization to keep cache lean
07:52 Marcus: exactly — summarization + indexed retrieval pattern recommended: keep only recent few hundred tokens in KV cache and use embeddings store for long-term history at retrieval time
08:05 Lucas: can the cost model include embeddings + extra storage?
08:09 Marcus: yes, our spreadsheet has lines for embedding storage, retrieval latency, and extra compute; we can customize with your S3 costs and vector DB assumptions
08:18 Priya: what's a realistic timeline for a POC?
08:21 Olivia: typical POC is 4–6 weeks: week 1 instrumentation and trace export, week 2 baseline runs + config, weeks 3–4 leaderboard/iterative tuning, final week for handoff and pricing discussion
08:33 Marcus: we'll propose a benchmarking plan in the spreadsheet.
08:35 Olivia: quick demo — Marcus can show console where we simulate batch/coalescing curves
08:42 Marcus: screen share starts (note: transcription may miss some UI labels) — here's the console simulate tab, upload trace, set batch ceilings, toggle KV cache and TTL. With their sample we see p95 drop from 950 to 420 and cost per 1k calls from $18 to $9 with cache + batching + int8 quantization
09:12 Priya: that $9 number assumes what model?
09:15 Marcus: a mid-sized 30B variant quantized int8 and an 8xA100 equivalent pricing — we will swap to your cloud SKUs when we run the POC
09:22 Evan: are the benchmarking scripts intrusive? we can't risk hitting prod DBs
09:26 Marcus: non-intrusive — we replay traces against a sandbox model endpoint and can point requests at a canary with synthetic data; we never write to your prod DB unless you opt in to integration tests
09:37 Marta: send security questionnaire, also need IP subnets for peering
09:41 Olivia: will do. okay wrapping up, let's capture next steps
09:48 Priya: quick q — when you run the POC can you highlight token-level cost per route in the dashboard?
09:52 Marcus: yes the dashboard breaks down token-level cost, latency, and cache hit rate per route and per model variant
09:58 Olivia: recap: we'll send cost model spreadsheet + SOC2/private deploy docs, Marcus will prepare benchmark scripts and a sample trace simulation, Evan will share traces and infra constraints, Marta will review security docs. target: schedule 2-hour benchmark Wed 2026-03-18 10am PT.
10:18 Priya: sounds good thanks everyone
10:22 Olivia: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links
10:26 [call ends]
